insider_note: Both brackets share the common factor x and y respectively — pulling that factor out first is what turns this equation into a separable one, rather than trying to treat it as a homogeneous equation.

steps.label: Recognise the separable form
steps.margin_note: One mark. Factor x out of the first bracket and y out of the second before rearranging.
steps.memory_tip: xy² + x = x(y² + 1); yx² + y = y(x² + 1) — both brackets factor the same way.
lines: The given D.E is (xy² + x)dx + (yx² + y)dy = 0
This equation is in the variables-separable
steps.why: Factoring x out of the first bracket and y out of the second reveals that each bracket only depends on one variable, which is the sign that x and y can be fully separated to opposite sides.
common_mistakes: Not factoring out x and y first, and instead attempting the y = vx homogeneous substitution.
Factoring incorrectly as x(y² − 1) instead of x(y² + 1).

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Move the y-terms to the right side and divide by (x²+1)(y²+1).
steps.memory_tip: Divide the whole equation by (x²+1)(y²+1) to send x-terms and y-terms to opposite sides.
steps.why: Dividing both sides by (x² + 1)(y² + 1) leaves x and its differential entirely on one side and y and its differential entirely on the other, which is exactly what separation of variables requires.
common_mistakes: Dividing only one bracket instead of both, leaving a mixed x and y term.
Losing the minus sign when moving the y(x²+1)dy term across the equals sign.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: One mark. Both sides are the standard ∫x/(x²+1)dx = (1/2)log(x²+1) shape.
steps.memory_tip: The numerator on each side is exactly half the derivative of the denominator — a direct log-integral.
steps.why: Both integrals are the standard form ∫(a fraction whose numerator is half the derivative of its denominator), giving a log of the denominator directly; combining the two logs on the same side keeps the next step simple.
common_mistakes: Missing the factor of 1/2 in front of each log.
Leaving the equation with logs on both sides instead of combining them onto one side before the next step.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Remove the log by exponentiating both sides.
steps.memory_tip: log(A) = log(B) means A = B directly — no further algebra is needed once the logs match.
steps.why: Once both sides are written as a single log, equal logs mean the quantities inside are equal, giving the final relation between x, y and the constant directly.
common_mistakes: Writing the final answer as x² + y² = c, dropping the +1 terms and the product structure.
Leaving the log on the left side instead of exponentiating to remove it.
